I think a big part of the thing is that people are missing why these things are so incredibly expensive in America. America has vastly more expensive education than just about anywhere else in the developed world. We spend vastly more per capita on healthcare than anywhere else in the developed world. Even on smaller things, America also has vastly more expensive internet than more or less anywhere in the developed world. And it's not because we get a better product. Our healthcare outcomes are relatively poor relative to the rest of the world, our internet access standards are a joke compared to the rest of the world, and while our universities are still top notch - we're beginning a downward slide there as well.

Now there's one huge difference in our markets in these fields relative to the rest of the world, and it's hugely ironic. Relative to the rest of the world the market in these industries is very poorly regulated. There are minimal to no pricing/service controls and when you let major players control life-critical industries they have the power to jack up their prices to however much they want. Think about something like the fire department. That is an almost entirely nationalized industry. And it's a hell of a great service. If your house is on fire the fire department's going to be there to put it out and you pay next to nothing to keep those departments in service. Imagine it was a private industry. How much are you willing to pay to protect your house? Whatever the answer is, it's a whole lot more than you currently pay and that's what you'd end up paying if it was a private industry.

Because the issue in capitalism is that companies aren't stupid. The free market is incredible if companies would just agree to grind each other into the ground in a race to the bottom of pricing. But no, they have long since realized that they earn a whole lot more money simply colluding and instead of spending their money developing their product - they use it to keep out competitors. Make deals that undercut their supply chain, buy them up, whatever. Especially in fields where there are significant barriers to entry, they end up in a position to print money.

So thinking you'd pay more when these industries end up being 'half-nationalized' really just isn't accurate. He is also radically understating wealth inequality. Right now in the US the top 0.1% have as much wealth as the bottom 90%!!!! Please note the source of that article before you think this is some political spin - this is the real state of the country we live in. Think about that for a minute. If the US was 1000 people in a room, one guy would have as much as the bottom 900 people combined. And that wealth inequality is rapidly growing. We'd almost certainly end up paying less as a society, and the 'average joe' would see minimal to no economic burden. The super wealthy would certainly see an increased economic burden in the short term, yet these changes would vastly improve the longterm outlook of the US and the longterm is presumably where the economic elite of this country are looking to. The economic kings in a country of paupers are akin to being the smartest kid on the short bus. That's not good for anybody.

I think I already hit reasonably well on the reasons for the lower prices. To be clear though single payer systems for healthcare or other fields don't mean the government 'handles healthcare' in the fashion you're talking about. Right now Obamacare is a joke. It's effectively encoded into law that private citizens are forced to pay private middlemen who provide absolutely no service other than taking a very large cut of all money before handing it along to the hospitals. Single payer means you pay the government who then directly pays the hospitals - effectively working as a national level insurer.

I also think you're missing the most important reason that "college is the new high school." We're definitely more educated but not 'that' much more. In 1977 we reached a peak of 24% of people having a 4 year degree or more. In 2014 (latest numbers from the census) it was 34%. The thing you're not considering is worker productivity. I think this graph tells the story pretty clearly. That entire article is full of intriguing data: http://www.epi.org/publication/charting-wage-stagnation/

Worker productivity has been skyrocketing. And with increasing automation we're likely to see potentially exponential growth there. In the 50s you might have needed 50 skilled workers to provide the goods and services for 100 people. Now those same 50 people can provide the goods and services for 300 people! As worker productivity increases, the required number of workers to maintain production decreases. We're not only seeing people with college degrees working fastfood in today's economy, but we're also seeing record lows in the workforce participation rate. The jobs aren't there anymore because companies don't need anywhere near as many workers to maintain productivity anymore. This is also why even though workers are earning companies vastly more per hour, their wages have hardly changed. Since companies don't need as many workers, the ones they do have have become disposable. Not happy with your wages? Well you don't have to worry about that anymore - you're fired. Now I'll go hire the kid with an degree working at Starbucks.

And education itself is critical for pushing a society forward. Uneducated individuals essentially by definition are going to make less appropriate decisions than educated individuals. Trying to strive for this as a means of fixing our economy is myopic. Even on the micro scale, imagine if somebody like Elon Musk was never able to prosper since he wasn't born to a family with the capacity to provide him access to education in a country where education became class based. That'd be a shame not just for him but for all of humanity. You never know where the next innovator is going to come from.

Coney (which is ultimately derived from the Latin cuniculus) entered the English language c. 1200, via French.

Over the years, puns based on the words coney (which originally rhymed with honey rather than bony) and cunt became increasingly common. From a play written in 1622:

A pox on your Christian cockatrices! They cry, like poulterers’ wives, ‘No money, no coney’.

By the 1800s, the word had become so taboo that it had gradually been replaced with the word rabbit, which originally referred to the young of the species. Since the word coney couldn’t be dropped altogether (it was in the King James Bible, for example) the solution was to change the pronunciation to the form we use today.
The word "coney" (meaning "rabbit") fell out of use because it became associated with the word "cunt."
